step.text:
Looking at Electron 33's notification implementation, the `Show()` method closes any existing notification before creating a new one through the presenter, generating a unique ID for it. The `Notification` class itself is wrapped with cleanup-at-exit semantics, which handles garbage collection when the process terminates.

There's a known issue where notification click events don't fire if the JS wrapper gets garbage collected — the native observer gets destroyed along with it. On macOS specifically, when the JS object is GC'd, the destructor calls `set_delegate(nullptr)` and destroys the notification, which on older macOS versions would remove it from the notification center entirely. But since Jamel can still click the notification, it's likely either not being GC'd or the banner persists on screen even after removal from the delivered list. With newer UNUserNotificationCenter (macOS 11+, used in Electron v25+), the behavior around notification removal might differ.

The symptom — "clicking just hides the notification" — is exactly what happens when the app receives no click callback: macOS dismisses the banner on click by default without the delegate firing. If the `click` event were actually firing, `openWindow()` would focus the window, which Jamel would definitely notice. Since he reports nothing happens, the click event isn't being triggered at all.

Two main possibilities: either the Notification object is being garbage collected because no reference is held, or macOS isn't routing the default action to an unsigned dev-run app — though if that were the case, Jamel wouldn't be seeing the notification appear in the first place.

I'm leaning toward the GC issue. The fix would be to hold a reference to each notification until it's closed or clicked, then release it. I should also check how the app handles the window creation timing and whether the renderer is ready when the notification fires. Let me look at the test coverage for alerts and see if there's a main-process test harness, and also verify how Electron 33 handles notification garbage collection.

+ export type Box = { left: number; width: number }
+ 
+ const end = (box: Box) => box.left + box.width
+ const middle = (box: Box) => box.left + box.width / 2
+ 
+ // The room one leaves behind when it is lifted out of the row: its own width and
+ // the gap beside it, read off the row itself rather than from the class that set
+ // the gap, so nothing here has to be told the number twice.
+ export function room(boxes: Box[], from: number): number {
+   const held = boxes[from]
+   if (!held) return 0
+   const after = boxes[from + 1]
+   const before = boxes[from - 1]
+   const gap = after ? after.left - end(held) : before ? held.left - end(before) : 0
+   return held.width + gap
+ }
+ 
+ // Where one dragged dx from its own slot would land. The leading edge is what
+ // decides it rather than the middle: measured from the middle, a wide one has to
+ // travel its own width as well as the gap before it passes the narrow one beside
+ // it, which reads as a row that will not take what is being dragged into it.
+ export function landing(boxes: Box[], from: number, dx: number): number {
+   const held = boxes[from]
+   if (!held) return from
+   let to = from
+   boxes.forEach((box, index) => {
+     if (index > from && end(held) + dx > middle(box)) to = Math.max(to, index)
+     if (index < from && held.left + dx < middle(box)) to = Math.min(to, index)
+   })
+   return to
+ }
+ 
+ // How far the one standing at index steps aside while from is on its way to to.
+ // Everything the held one has passed moves back by the room it left behind, and
+ // every gap is the same width, so one number covers all of them.
+ export function shift(boxes: Box[], from: number, to: number, index: number): number {
+   if (index > from && index <= to) return -room(boxes, from)
+   if (index < from && index >= to) return room(boxes, from)
+   return 0
+ }

+ import { useRef, type PointerEvent as Press } from 'react'
+ import { landing, shift, type Box } from './reorder'
+ 
+ // How far the pointer travels before the row believes it is a drag rather than a
+ // press, so a plain click still lands on whatever it was aimed at.
+ const TAKES = 4
+ // A row that scrolls carries itself along while something is held near either end
+ // of it, or the far end is somewhere nothing can be dropped.
+ const EDGE = 56
+ const STEP = 12
+ const SLIDE = 'translate 150ms cubic-bezier(0.4, 0, 0.2, 1)'
+ 
+ export type Reorder = {
+   ref: (node: HTMLElement | null) => void
+   take(id: string): (event: Press) => void
+   dragged(): boolean
+ }
+ 
+ // Dragging one of a row of things into another place in it. Where each one goes
+ // is written straight onto the elements rather than held in state, the way the
+ // music's bars are: it runs every frame, and a render a frame would cost
+ // everything standing beside the row. Nothing is reordered until it is let go,
+ // so the row under the pointer stands still while it is being aimed at.
+ export function useReorder(onMove: (id: string, to: number) => void): Reorder {
+   const row = useRef<HTMLElement | null>(null)
+   const dragged = useRef(false)
+ 
+   const take = (id: string) => (event: Press) => {
+     const strip = row.current
+     if (event.button !== 0 || !strip) return
+     const bar = strip.getBoundingClientRect()
+     const items = Array.from(strip.querySelectorAll<HTMLElement>('[data-reorder]'))
+     const from = items.findIndex(item => item.dataset.reorder === id)
+     const held = items[from]
+     if (!held || items.length < 2) return
+ 
+     // Boxes are read in the row's own coordinates rather than the window's, so a
+     // row that scrolls under a drag does not put every one of them out.
+     const boxes: Box[] = items.map(item => {
+       const box = item.getBoundingClientRect()
+       return { left: box.left - bar.left + strip.scrollLeft, width: box.width }
+     })
+     const startX = event.clientX - bar.left + strip.scrollLeft
+ 
+     let pointer = event.clientX
+     let taken = false
+     let to = from
+     let frame = 0
+     dragged.current = false
+ 
+     const tick = () => {
+       const dx = pointer - bar.left + strip.scrollLeft - startX
+       if (!taken && Math.abs(dx) < TAKES) return
+       taken = true
+       dragged.current = true
+       held.style.translate = `${dx}px`
+       held.style.zIndex = '10'
+       held.style.cursor = 'grabbing'
+       const next = landing(boxes, from, dx)
+       if (next === to) return
+       to = next
+       items.forEach((item, index) => {
+         if (index === from) return
+         item.style.transition = SLIDE
+         item.style.translate = `${shift(boxes, from, to, index)}px`
+       })
+     }
+ 
+     // The pointer standing still near an end still carries the row along, so the
+     // reading happens on a frame of its own as well as on every move.
+     const draw = () => {
+       frame = requestAnimationFrame(draw)
+       const past = pointer - bar.left
+       if (past < EDGE) strip.scrollLeft -= STEP
+       else if (past > bar.width - EDGE) strip.scrollLeft += STEP
+       tick()
+     }
+ 
+     const move = (moved: PointerEvent) => {
+       pointer = moved.clientX
+       tick()
+     }
+ 
+     // Everything the drag wrote is taken off before the row is reordered, and
+     // the transition goes with it, or the one that was let go slides in from a
+     // slot it has already left.
+     const stop = (keep: boolean) => {
+       cancelAnimationFrame(frame)
+       window.removeEventListener('pointermove', move)
+       window.removeEventListener('pointerup', up)
+       window.removeEventListener('pointercancel', cancel)
+       window.removeEventListener('keydown', key)
+       items.forEach(item => {
+         item.style.translate = ''
+         item.style.transition = ''
+         item.style.zIndex = ''
+         item.style.cursor = ''
+       })
+       if (keep && to !== from) onMove(id, to)
+     }
+ 
+     const up = () => stop(true)
+     const cancel = () => stop(false)
+     const key = (pressed: KeyboardEvent) => {
+       if (pressed.key === 'Escape') stop(false)
+     }
+ 
+     window.addEventListener('pointermove', move)
+     window.addEventListener('pointerup', up)
+     window.addEventListener('pointercancel', cancel)
+     window.addEventListener('keydown', key)
+     frame = requestAnimationFrame(draw)
+   }
+ 
+   return {
+     ref: node => {
+       row.current = node
+     },
+     take,
+     dragged: () => dragged.current
+   }
+ }

I can't verify this empirically without manual interaction, so let me check Electron's C++ source code instead—specifically the notification implementation in the main process to understand how references are managed.

Looking at the Show method and destructor, I see that `notification_` is a weak pointer, and when the JS Notification object gets garbage collected, the delegate is set to null. This means when macOS reports a click, the native notification presenter tries to call the delegate but finds nothing there—the click gets swallowed while the banner still dismisses. This is exactly the symptom, and it's a well-documented footgun with `gin::Wrappable` objects that lose their JS references.

The garbage collection likely happens within seconds since the main process runs idle-time GC while the notification sits on screen. There's also the detail that the native notification gets removed from the notification center when the JS object is destroyed, but since the presenter owns the native notification, the banner stays visible—consistent with what we're seeing.

So the core fix is to keep the notification alive until it's actually clicked or closed, and also handle the case where the window doesn't exist yet or multiple windows are open and we're targeting the wrong one.

I should refactor `openWindow()` to return the BrowserWindow and create a helper that sends the thread open event immediately if the window's already loaded, or waits for `did-finish-load` if it's still initializing. I need to verify that `createWindow()` actually returns the window object, and also check whether `alert.threadId` might be undefined for mention alerts since only `finishedAlert` sets it. I'm also wondering what test coverage exists for this notification flow.

So `createUpdateInfoTasks` actually runs independently of the `isPublish` flag—it's controlled by `event.isWriteUpdateInfo` and whether `publishConfigs` exists. This means even with `--publish never`, the update info files like `latest-mac.yml` and `latest.yml` still get written as long as there's a publish config in package.json. There's one thing to watch though: `getPublishConfigs` takes `this.isPublish` as an error handling parameter, so when `isPublish` is false it won't throw an error.

I've also confirmed that `getAppUpdatePublishConfiguration` writes the `app-update.yml` file into the packaged app's resources—that's what electron-updater reads at runtime to find the update server. It's gated on having darwin targets with dmg or zip (we have both), and since it's called with `errorIfCannot = false`, it won't throw if something's missing. The config resolves correctly because we've explicitly set the owner and repo in the publish section.

I need to keep notifications alive in the alerts module until they're explicitly clicked or closed, so I'll track them in a set and remove them when those events fire. The tricky part is that Electron's `close` event isn't guaranteed to fire on all platforms—macOS especially has inconsistent behavior—so I need to be careful about relying on it as the sole cleanup mechanism.

I'm thinking about adding a timeout ceiling to prevent unbounded growth over a long session. A reasonable approach is to keep a small set of active notifications and cap it at something like 20 entries, dropping the oldest ones when the limit is exceeded. This mirrors the toast stack pattern and keeps memory usage bounded without being overly aggressive about invalidating old notifications that might still be clickable in the Notification Center.

But before I ship this fix, I should verify that garbage collection is actually the culprit. I can write a test using `FinalizationRegistry` to detect when the Notification wrapper gets collected, force GC, and confirm whether the native delegate is still alive—that would prove the current code allows the wrapper to be garbage collected while the notification remains on screen, and that my fix prevents that.

The cleanest approach is to avoid calling `.show()` on a real notification (which would spam Jamel's machine). step.text:
Added it. `crew` in a terminal opens Crew on the folder you are standing in.

**The command** is `bin/crew.mjs`: plain node, no dependencies, no build step, with a `bin` entry in `package.json` so `npm link` in this checkout puts it on PATH (or symlink the file into somewhere on PATH yourself).

```
crew [folder] [options]
  -n, --name <name>   the name you go by
      --in-project    keep the chat, docs and designs in the project
      --in-app        keep them in the Crew app, and write nothing into the project
      --share         let people on your network in
      --no-share      keep it to this machine
  -j, --join <link>   join a crew, and work in this folder
  -h, --help          -v, --version
```

The folder is the one you are in unless you name another, relative paths resolve from where you ran it, and `--join` is refused `--share`, `--in-project` and `--in-app` because those belong to whoever hosts. `CREW_APP` picks which Crew to open, otherwise the installed app, otherwise the one built in this checkout.

**How it reaches the app.** The command works the request out and hands it over as one flag, `--crew-open=` with JSON, rather than a row of flags the app would have to learn a second time. `cleanOpenRequest` in `src/shared/cli.ts` keeps the folder, name, home, share and link and drops everything else. Main reads it once and clears it, and skips resuming the last session while one is waiting so the two cannot race. `follow` in `Home.tsx` then walks the same path a press on a row does: no name goes to the name screen and comes back, an unknown project gets the one question, a known one opens straight away.

**Documented** in `AGENTS.md` under a new "The crew command" section, with the reasoning behind each of those decisions, plus a line in the top command list.

Checked: `tests/crew-cli.test.ts` (16 tests, passing) covers the parsing, the error cases, the app lookup and a round trip of a real request through both halves, which is what pins the flag written down on each side. `tests/home-recent-probe.test.ts` still passes, `yarn build` builds, and I drove the launcher against a stand-in app to confirm what it spawns. I did not open a real window from the command line here, since that would start a second host on this live folder while everyone is working, so give it a run yourself when you want to see it. Two `tsc` errors in `AddMenu.tsx`/`Attachments.tsx` and two in `tests/window-chrome.test.ts` are someone else's in-flight edits, not from this change.
